{{Short description|Theorem in probability theory}}
'''Raikov’s theorem,''' named for Russian mathematician [[Dmitrii Abramovich Raikov]], is a result in the [[probability theory]]. It is well known that if each of two [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] [[random variables]] <math>\xi_1</math> and <math>\xi_2</math> has a [[Poisson distribution]], then their sum <math>\xi = \xi_1 + \xi_2</math> has a Poisson distribution as well. It turns out that the converse is also valid.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Raikov
 |first=D. A.
 |year=1937
 |title=On the decomposition of Poisson laws
 |journal=Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR
 |volume=14
 |pages=9–12
}}</ref>

== Statement of the theorem ==
Suppose that a random variable <math>\xi</math> has a Poisson distribution and admits a decomposition as a sum <math>\xi = \xi_1 + \xi_2</math> of two independent random variables. Then the distribution  of each summand is a shifted Poisson distribution.

Raikov's theorem is similar to [[Cramér’s decomposition theorem]]. The latter result claims that if a sum of two independent random variables has a [[normal distribution]], then each summand is normally distributed as well. It was also proved by [[Yuri Linnik|Yu. V. Linnik]] that a convolution of normal distribution and Poisson's distribution possesses a similar property ({{ill|Linnik's theorem on convolution of normal distribution and Poisson's distribution|lt=Linnik's theorem|ru|Теорема Линника о разложении свертки нормального распределения и распределения Пуассона}}).
It follows from the Raikov theorem that the Poisson distribution belongs to the [[Linnik class|Linnik class <math>I_0</math>]].

== An extension to locally compact Abelian groups ==
Let  <math>X</math> be a [[Locally compact abelian group|locally compact Abelian group]]. Denote by <math>M^1(X)</math> the convolution [[semigroup]] of probability distributions on <math>X</math>, and by <math>E_x</math>the [[degenerate distribution]] concentrated at <math>x\in X</math>. Let <math>x_0\in X, \lambda>0</math>.

The Poisson distribution generated by the measure <math>\lambda E_{x_0}</math> is defined as a  distribution of the form

<div class="center">
<math>\mu=e(\lambda E_{x_0})=e^{-\lambda} \left( E_0+\lambda E_{x_0}+ \frac{\lambda^2 E_{2x_0}}{2!} + \cdots+ \frac{\lambda^n E_{nx_0}}{n!}+\cdots \right).
</math>
</div>

'''Theorem'''<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Rukhin
 |first=A. L.
 |year=1970
 |title=Certain statistical and probability problems on groups
 |journal=Proceedings of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics
 |volume=111
 |pages=59–129
}}</ref>
Let <math>\mu</math> be the Poisson distribution generated by the measure <math>\lambda E_{x_0}</math>. Suppose that <math>\mu=\mu_1*\mu_2</math>, with <math>\mu_j\in M^1(X)</math>. 
Then each of <math>\mu_j</math> is a shift of a Poisson  distribution  if 
and only if  <math>x_0</math> is either an infinite-order element  or has order 2.
